To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) 83.6 % of patients who receive a primary diagnosis of HIV during hospitalization present to care within 90 days of hospital discharge; and 2) immigrants from countries with a generalized HIV epidemic are more likely, whereas women and those with a mental health diagnosis are less likely to present to out-patient care within 90 days of hospital discharge.

1) among 372 patients who were diagnosed with HIV during their hospital admission in Ontario between April 1st, 2007 to March 31st, 2015, 83.5% presented to HIV care within 90 days of hospital discharge, and 2) among 483 patients diagnosed with HIV in hospital, but for whom HIV infection was not recorded as their primary diagnosis, 73.5% presented within 90 days.

1) Among people diagnosed with HIV during a hospitalization, presentation to care by three months after hospital discharge was common (83.6%); and 2) among those diagnosed with HIV but without a principal HIV diagnosis, immigrants from countries with a generalized HIV epidemic were more likely to be timely presenters to care, whereas women, people with mental health diagnoses, and people with a history of hospitalization for a substance use disorder were less likely to be timely.
